questions.title: Planning an experiment — oscillations of a bar suspended by strings

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer:
Apparatus: rod fixed horizontally to two stands with bosses and clamps on a bench; solid bar of mass M suspended from the rod by two equal vertical strings at equal distances a from its centre; metre rule, stopwatch, balance, spirit level.
Measurements: measure a (string to centre of bar) and L (rod to bar) with a rule; measure M with a balance. Displace one end of the bar horizontally by a small amount, release it and measure the time t for n oscillations (n is at least 5) with a stopwatch; T = t/n. Repeat for the same a and average T. Vary a over a wide range of values, keeping L constant, and repeat the procedure.
Analysis: plot a graph of lg T against lg a. Since T = 2πP√(a^q M/L), lg T = lg(2πP√(M/L)) + (q/2)lg a, so the graph is a straight line of gradient q/2. Hence q = 2 × gradient, and the y-intercept = lg(2πP√(M/L)), giving P = 10^(y-intercept) × √(L/M)/(2π). The relationship is valid if a straight line is obtained (it need not pass through the origin).
Control of variables: keep L and M constant; measure each a from the centre of the bar (e.g. measure the length of the bar, divide by two and mark the midpoint); keep the bar horizontal (spirit level) and the strings vertical (set square or plumb line); prevent the strings from sliding (adhesive putty, notches or grooves); use small-amplitude oscillations and a fiducial marker at the midpoint; use a large L to increase T and reduce its percentage uncertainty; repeat timings for the same a and average T.
Safety: G-clamp the stands to the bench (or load them with heavy weights) and place cushions or a sand tray on the bench below the bar, so that the bar or rod cannot fall and injure anyone.

questions.title: Falling steel ball in a liquid — density & terminal velocity

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: t = z / (gd²(ρ − σ)/18β) = (18βz/g(ρ − σ)) × (1/d²), so the graph of t against 1/d² is a straight line through the origin with gradient = 18βz/(g(ρ − σ)).

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.answer: Plot all six points of t against 1/d², each within half a small square of its true position, with point diameter less than half a small square (ecf from (b)). Add vertical error bars in 1/d² to all six points, symmetrical, with total length accurate to less than half a small square.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.answer: Draw the straight line of best fit — it must pass between (0.064, 2.50) and (0.066, 2.50), and between (0.134, 5.50) and (0.138, 5.50); label it. Draw the worst acceptable line — the steepest or shallowest line that passes through all the error bars; label it.

parts.label: (c)(iii)
parts.answer:
Gradient of best-fit line, with clear substitution of two data points separated by more than half the length of the line:
G = (6.10 − 1.45)/(0.148 − 0.040) = 4.65/0.108 = 43 s mm² (expect 36–48).
Absolute uncertainty = |gradient of best fit − gradient of worst acceptable line| (or ½(steepest − shallowest)) = ±1 s mm² (example).

parts.label: (e)(i)
parts.answer:
From (a): β = gradient × g(ρ − σ)/(18z), with z = 0.097 m and gradient = 43 s mm² = 4.3×10⁻⁵ s m².
β = 4.3×10⁻⁵ × 9.81 × 6600/(18 × 0.097) = 2.78/1.746 = 1.6 kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹ (expect ≈ 1.5; also accept 0.0015 kg mm⁻¹ s⁻¹, 1.5 g mm⁻¹ s⁻¹, Pa s or N m⁻² s).

parts.label: (e)(ii)
parts.answer:
Percentage uncertainty in β, with method shown:
%β = 100% × (ΔG/G + Δ(ρ − σ)/(ρ − σ) + Δz/z)
= 100% × (1/43 + 100/6600 + 2/97) = 100% × (0.023 + 0.0152 + 0.0206) ≈ 5.9% (must be greater than 2%; the density and z terms alone give ≈ 3.5%).
